prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength are interrogated free of Doppler and recoil shifts, bringing frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level.

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B020 to B024 alone, Katori and Ye. The reason is my own test, applied to my own first choice. I said at the outset that the committee must be absolutely sure it has identified the topic and the people who did the original work. For the optical lattice clock I can state the original idea (Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first lattice clock), the first demonstrations, and the record performance that followed, and the result has been reproduced and compared between many independent laboratories. The instrument opened a door in the sense I care about: thousands of atoms interrogated free of Doppler and recoil shifts at 10^-18 stability, which turns gravitational redshift over centimetres, drifting constants and dark-matter searches into laboratory questions. The comb gave the ruler and the single-ion work gave the single-particle clock, but neither gave this regime, and I think a citation worded around the magic-wavelength lattice keeps it distinct from the 2005 and 2012 citations. B020 remains for me the most exciting physics on the list, and I would still put it first on scientific novelty, but on the criteria of verified, original and clearly attributed it is not yet ready.
statement.case_against: Three weaknesses remain. First, lineage: no one, including me, has yet laid the 2005 and 2012 citation texts beside this one, and the instrument-versus-discovery question is real. Second, I said in round 1 that Ye's contribution is closer to the later, better experiment than to the original one. I now think that is too narrow, since the group demonstrated the strontium lattice clock at about the same time and then carried it to the best accuracy and into many-body clock physics, but the priority history is from memory and the committee should have it checked. Third, the redefinition of the second has not happened, and SYRTE, PTB and NIST contributions to the systematics are not credited. I do not think any of these is disqualifying, but I would not want to vote without the expert note that Kroll, Lindroth and the chair have asked for.

responses.point: Mehlig asked whether the lattice clock demonstrates a new physical principle or only a new level of precision, said the central idea was only partly unexpected whereas for flat bands the answer is yes, and pressed on Cao's absence from the B020 credit.
responses.response: I agree with your test, and it is the reason I am still torn. Flat bands pass it more clearly than the clock. But I now weigh the second half of the question more heavily: who made the decisive original experiment. For B020 the 2018 experiments were led at the bench by Yuan Cao, with Jarillo-Herrero as group leader, and with a three-name limit and a field eight years old I cannot say I am absolutely sure. I accept that group-leader credit is Academy practice, but it is a judgement call I am unwilling to rest a prize on this year. For the clock the principle is partly new, as you say, but the capability is new in kind and the credit is clean. I would be happy to see B020 return when the credit and the mechanism are better understood.

responses.point: Pearce keeps B019 (Halzen alone) as a second part but says it should be the first thing dropped if one name for IceCube cannot be defended, leaving B024 alone.
responses.response: I answer the chair's first question directly: no, I cannot defend Halzen as the sole credited laureate. The instrument is the achievement and I accept your point, but a detector built and analysed by hundreds, with AMANDA preceding it, needs a credited set that the shortlist does not supply, and I would not add names from outside it. So I agree with your own fallback and will not support the two-part prize; the part I support is the one you would keep. I also agree with you that the lattice concept is distinct from the combs and ion clocks, and I would want the citation to say magic-wavelength lattice explicitly.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice clock gave a regime that neither the 2005 nor the 2012 prize gave, asks for an outside check of the 1e-18 figures and priority history, and discloses a distant Hall-lab link to Jun Ye.
responses.response: I now agree that the lattice clock gave a regime that the earlier prizes did not. Your disclosure is distant and I would not treat it as disqualifying, but it should be recorded. The expert note you ask for should be requested before the final ballot. In particular I want the primary record on three points: the date and content of Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, the first strontium lattice demonstrations from Katori's and Ye's groups, and the first clock-to-clock comparisons at the 10^-18 level. My change of position depends on that record holding.

responses.point: Eriksson would not oppose B020 as the whole prize but is willing to move to B024 if the committee finds the moire field too immature, and wants the experimental credit stated openly.
responses.response: I take your willingness to move as meeting me halfway. I do not think the moire mechanism is the problem: a citation can be worded around the flat-band prediction and the observed phases, as you and I both argued. My problem is the credit for the 2018 experiments, and that is a record question, not a question of taste. If the record shows that group-leader attribution is the Academy's established practice here, I would reconsider B020 in a later year. I would ask that it stay in the minutes as a strong candidate.

uncertainties: Whether the 2005 and 2012 citation texts, read against the proposed B024 citation, leave the magic-wavelength lattice clock distinct enough; I rely on my recollection of them.

The priority history of the magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium lattice demonstrations, and whether Ye's credit rests on the original idea or on the record accuracy; the 10^-18 figures are from recollection and need an outside check.
Whether the committee would prefer to wait for the formal redefinition of the second, and whether that standard would also be applied to the younger moire materials.
Whether B020 may be ready in a later year if the 2018 experimental credit (Yuan Cao and device work by other groups) is settled and the mechanism clarifies.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for Katori, Ye or B024. I work in electron microscopy and materials and have no stated collaboration with either name or their groups. I support the disclosures by Johansson, Kroll, Lindroth and Pearce being recorded as they stand, and, as in round 1, I would support Johansson's recusal from the attribution on B042. Gothenburg/Chalmers proximity to Johansson and Mehlig is institutional only, and neither of my preferred ballots involves them.
